FrMS88-de4898-d1e110.summary: Title of the fourteenth question: whether theology is a science.

FrMS88-de4898-d1e118.summary: Opening argument: Augustine (De Trinitate) assigns action to science and contemplation to wisdom; theology is not an active habit, so it is not a science.
claims: Objection: science concerns action, while theology is contemplative.

FrMS88-de4898-d1e125.summary: Contrary: Augustine himself attributes (certain things) to 'this science'.

FrMS88-de4898-d1e130.summary: Announces that the question will first address the meaning of the terms.

FrMS88-de4898-d1e138.summary: Second, it will investigate the truth. Begins with the term 'theology', which has four senses: the habit of those to whom it was revealed (prophets and saints, who per Dionysius taught us to praise God in all creatures); the habit generated in us by study of Scripture; the habit deduced from truths contained in Scripture; and the habit declaring and defending the faith (of which Jerome speaks). In the first sense, it was evident and certain.
claims: Theology has four senses.
Revealed theology in the prophets was evident and certain.

FrMS88-de4898-d1e167.summary: Raises the great doubt how the prophets had certainty. One answer: from the major 'God cannot lie' with the minor 'God said this'.
claims: Reported view: prophetic certitude rests on the syllogism 'God cannot lie; God said this'.

FrMS88-de4898-d1e178.summary: Objects that the minor ('God said this') is not evident: no contingent truth can be known with certainty unless at least one extreme is known intuitively, since abstractive cognition through a species represents the thing equally whether it exists or not; but none of them knew God or his speech intuitively.
claims: Contingent truths are certainly known only through intuitive cognition of at least one extreme.
Abstractive cognition represents its object indifferently to existence.

FrMS88-de4898-d1e207.summary: Reports another answer: the prophets had a supernatural light greater than that of faith and less than that of glory.
claims: Reported view: prophets had a light intermediate between faith and glory.

FrMS88-de4898-d1e214.summary: Objects: when a habitude follows from the formal notions of the terms, in whatever light the terms are known the habitude is known; the prophets had the same theological terms we have, so the same light would reveal the habitude, and a third light is useless.
claims: Knowledge of a habitude grounded in its terms requires no light beyond that by which the terms are known.

FrMS88-de4898-d1e230.summary: Reports a further answer: the prophets had different terms.

FrMS88-de4898-d1e236.summary: Objects: what the prophets affirmed, the philosophers denied, so the philosopher denying and the theologian affirming had the same terms.
claims: Affirmation and denial of the same proposition presuppose the same terms.

FrMS88-de4898-d1e243.summary: Reports another answer: the prophets had an abstractive knowledge others lacked.

FrMS88-de4898-d1e250.summary: Objects: this might suffice for necessary truths but not for contingent ones, since abstractive cognition abstracts from existence and cannot certify contingents.
claims: Abstractive cognition cannot certify contingent truths.

FrMS88-de4898-d1e259.summary: Concludes that the prophets' mode of certainty and evidence is unknown to us. Theology in the second sense is not science but faith; nor in the third sense, since conclusions from two believed premises, or one known and one believed, are believed, a conclusion following the weaker premise. In the fourth sense it is the noblest and highest part of metaphysics: metaphysics treats being as being (knowing of God only what follows being as such) and also the things under being, including God, the noblest; hence Augustine calls the Platonists theological philosophers.
claims: The prophets' mode of certitude is unknown to us.
A conclusion follows the weaker premise, so conclusions from believed premises are believed.
Theology as defense of the faith is the noblest part of metaphysics.

FrMS88-de4898-d1e296.summary: Lists seven conditions of science: it is cognition (unlike moral virtues), true (unlike opinion), evident (unlike enigmatic faith), habitual (unlike an act), necessary (unlike art and prudence), acquired by syllogistic discourse (unlike understanding of principles), and caused from self-evident principles.
claims: Science requires seven conditions distinguishing it from virtue, opinion, faith, act, art, prudence, and understanding of principles.

FrMS88-de4898-d1e316.summary: Draws two consequences: knowledge concluded from believed principles is not science, since a conclusion cannot be better known than its principles; and an angel, supposing it does not reason discursively, has no science.
claims: Knowledge from believed principles is not science.
An angel without discourse would have no science.

FrMS88-de4898-d1e328.summary: Raises a doubt whether the theologian by this habit can satisfy the philosopher; some say not.

FrMS88-de4898-d1e335.summary: Objects: the philosopher's argument errs either in form or matter; if in form, the form fails; if in matter, a premise is false, so the theologian can at least defend himself. Then turns to the term 'science', setting out four conclusions: it is a true and evident habit (unlike opinion and faith), necessary (unlike prudence and art), about what is not self-evident (unlike understanding of principles), and by syllogistic discourse. Raises four objections: demons and separated substances do not demonstrate; separated souls lack phantasms and cannot discourse; angels and the blessed have perfect science of the divine essence without discourse; and God, who does not discourse, would lack science.
claims: The theologian can always defend the faith against a philosopher's argument by locating its formal or material flaw.
Science is a true, evident, necessary habit about non-self-evident truths acquired by syllogistic discourse.
Objection: separated substances, the blessed, and God have science without discourse.

FrMS88-de4898-d1e385.summary: Reply to the first: it is accidental to science to be acquired by discourse in time; discourse can occur in an instant, and separated intellects discourse by order of nature, not of time.
claims: Discourse can be by order of nature in an instant.

FrMS88-de4898-d1e394.summary: Reply to the second: discourse through phantasms is accidental to science, belonging to the soul in its present state.
claims: Reliance on phantasms is accidental to science.

FrMS88-de4898-d1e401.summary: Reply to the third: it is not unfitting that angels and the blessed conclude infinity and other posterior truths from priors, namely the divine essence.
claims: The blessed can infer posterior truths from the divine essence.

FrMS88-de4898-d1e408.summary: Reply to the fourth: some hold that there can be discourse in God by reason, since there is a primary and secondary object and he knows the secondary through the primary — e.g. knowing through his essence that it is communicable to three persons, and knowing creatures' quiddities — and so he can have science.
claims: God can be said to have science by knowing secondary objects through his essence as primary object.

FrMS88-de4898-d1e427.summary: Raises four objections to this: a scientific intellect proceeds from more known to less known, unfitting in God; no intuitive knowledge is discursive and the blessed know intuitively; discourse involves several acts, while God and angels regarding God have one act; and whatever is intuitively known is self-evident and so cannot be demonstrated.
claims: Objection: intuitive, single-act knowledge excludes discourse.

FrMS88-de4898-d1e449.summary: Reply to the first: 'more known' can mean more certain in itself, which does not apply, or principal and prior, which does: God can 'discourse' from his essence as principally known to things secondarily known.
claims: God proceeds from his essence as principally known to secondarily known objects.

FrMS88-de4898-d1e465.summary: Reply to the second: intuitive knowledge is sometimes or can be discursive; Augustine (Super Genesim) says the blessed, knowing God, consequently know creatures, and so can be said to discourse in a way.
claims: Intuitive knowledge can involve a kind of discourse.

FrMS88-de4898-d1e476.summary: Reply to the third: separated spirits can know a whole discourse in one act, though this is not so for us now.
claims: Separated spirits can grasp a whole discourse in one act.

FrMS88-de4898-d1e483.summary: Reply to the fourth: what is intuitively known is self-evident and cannot be demonstrated within that knowledge, but can be through another formal notion — seeing the sun one sees it is round without demonstration, but one can demonstrate its roundness abstractively. Answers the question by distinguishing: theology as the habit the object can produce in a proportioned intellect is a science; as what the wayfarer's intellect can grasp it is not, since we cannot have certain knowledge of the object to know theological truths as theological; but metaphysical truths about God can be known scientifically.
claims: What is intuitively known can be demonstrated through another formal notion.
Theology in itself is a science; for the wayfarer, strictly theological truths are not scientifically known.
Metaphysical truths about God can be known scientifically by the wayfarer.

FrMS88-de4898-d1e522.summary: Reply to the opening argument: Augustine is not distinguishing science from wisdom there; he calls wisdom the science of eternal things.
claims: Augustine's wisdom is a science of eternal things.

FrMS88-de4898.summary: The fourteenth question of the prologue, turning from the theory of being to the status of theology, asks whether theology is a science. Meyronnes first clarifies the terms. 'Theology' has four senses: the revealed habit of prophets and saints; the habit acquired from studying Scripture; the habit deduced from scriptural truths; and the declarative and defensive habit of faith. The first was evident and certain, though how the prophets were certain of the contingent fact that God spoke remains unknown to us — he rejects explanations by the rule 'God cannot lie', by a light between faith and glory, by different terms, or by abstractive cognition. The second and third senses are faith, not science, since a conclusion follows the weaker premise; the fourth is the noblest part of metaphysics, the part concerning God among the things contained under being. 'Science' requires seven conditions (cognition, truth, evidence, habituality, necessity, syllogistic discourse, derivation from self-evident principles), so conclusions from believed principles are not science, and an angel without discourse would lack science. He defends the requirement of discourse against objections from separated substances, the blessed, and God, holding that discourse may be instantaneous and by order of nature, that the blessed infer posterior truths from the divine essence, and that God can 'discourse' from his essence as principally known to secondary objects. His answer: theology taken as the habit the object can cause in a proportioned intellect is a science; taken as what the wayfarer can attain, strictly theological truths are not known scientifically, though the metaphysical truths about God are. Augustine's opposition of science and wisdom is not at issue, since he calls wisdom the science of eternal things.
claims: 'Theology' can mean the revealed habit of the prophets, the acquired habit of Scripture study, the habit deduced from scriptural truths, or the defensive habit of faith.
The prophets' revealed knowledge was evident and certain, but the mode of that certainty is unknown to us.
Conclusions drawn from believed premises are believed, not scientifically known.
Theology as the defense of faith is the noblest part of metaphysics.
Science requires truth, evidence, necessity, habituality, syllogistic discourse, and self-evident principles.
Discourse required for science can be by order of nature rather than of time.
Theology is a science in itself, but not for the wayfarer with respect to properly theological truths.
